title: Gospel, Taizé and worship songs
hook: from Black gospel choirs to Taizé's repeated chants to modern worship bands

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Trisagion, holy, holy, holy, and then a plea for mercy, and your line was close to the ground. And this whole week: the tithe, pastors and money, alms, a stranger's welcome, and then the church singing. Today the week ends with music. Day one hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `CLOSE TO THE GROUND.` → `A WEEK OF GIVING AND SINGING.`

segments.voice: Three rooms, one Sunday. In the first, a choir in bright robes is swaying, a Hammond organ is growling, and a soloist holds one note until the whole church is on its feet. In the second, a church in a French village, young people from many countries are sitting on the floor in candlelight, singing the same short phrase over and over, quieter each time, until it feels like breathing. In the third, a converted warehouse, the lights go low, a drummer counts in, and a band plays while people raise their hands. Three sounds that could hardly be more different. And people in all three rooms might use the same word for it: prayer. Today's word names the first of them.
screen: `A CHOIR AND A HAMMOND ORGAN.` → `CANDLES AND ONE PHRASE, REPEATED.` → `A BAND IN A WAREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: Gospel. The word means good news, and it names a kind of music born in Black churches in America. It grew out of the spirituals we met two days ago, the blues and the energy of Pentecostal worship. The man often called its father is Thomas A. Dorsey, a Chicago blues pianist. His wife died giving birth, and their baby son died soon after. In that grief, he sat down at a piano and wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord. Mahalia Jackson sang it across the world, and it was sung at Martin Luther King Junior's funeral. Gospel music often comes out of the hardest places. Taizé is something else. It's a small community of brothers in a village in France, begun by Brother Roger, with members from Protestant and Catholic churches together. Young people come from many countries to spend a week there. Their songs are short: one line of scripture or prayer, sung again and again, sometimes in Latin, sometimes in many languages. The repetition is the point. The hope is that somewhere in the repeats, singers stop thinking about the words and start praying them. Then modern worship music: guitars, drums, songs sung straight to God, now a familiar sound in churches around the world. Not every church uses instruments. Orthodox worship is traditionally sung without them, and some Protestant churches, like the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied on purpose. Others use every instrument they can find, because Psalm 150 says, in the King James Bible: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Christians argue about music, sometimes loudly. But a choir, a chant and a band can all carry the same prayer.
screen: `GOSPEL: BORN IN BLACK CHURCHES.` · `DORSEY: PRECIOUS LORD, OUT OF GRIEF.` · `TAIZÉ: ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `WITH INSTRUMENTS, OR WITHOUT.` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. This week has been about giving, welcoming and singing. Now just listen. Settle, and breathe. Think of the style of church music that feels least like you: the gospel choir, the quiet chant, the loud band, the old organ. Imagine yourself in that room for a minute. Imagine the person next to you, for whom this is exactly how prayer sounds. Let yourself be curious rather than critical. If you pray, you can pray alongside them in your mind. Later today, listen to one piece of church music, any style. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. Good news, and a music born in Black churches in America, where grief and joy share one song.
Your line: every style can pray. Today, listen to one piece of church music, maybe in a style you'd never choose. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians sing in many styles: gospel choirs in many Black churches, Taizé chants at prayer services across denominations, contemporary worship bands in many Protestant churches, and unaccompanied chant in Orthodox and some Protestant churches.

original.note: Greek: good news. English gospel comes from the Old English for good news, gōdspel.

trapdoor: what you thought: gospel means church music with a big choir.
what it means: good news, and a music born in Black churches, where grief and joy share one song.
what a scholar hears: gospel music drew on spirituals, blues and Pentecostal worship; Thomas A. Dorsey helped shape it and publish it.

sources.quoted: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.

notes: Dorsey: wife Nettie died in childbirth in August 1932; the infant son died shortly after; Take My Hand, Precious Lord written soon after. Confirm.
Precious Lord at Martin Luther King Jr.'s funeral: Mahalia Jackson sang it at his funeral in 1968 (it was his request). Confirm.
Taizé: founded by Brother Roger (Roger Schütz) in 1940 in Taizé, Burgundy; ecumenical brothers from Protestant and Catholic backgrounds. Confirm. Taizé songs are copyrighted, so none are quoted.
Churches of Christ (a cappella) and Orthodox unaccompanied singing: generalizations; confirm wording ('many Orthodox churches').
Review segment looks back over week 20 (days 131–139), naming the tithe (day 131) and the widow's coins (day 132).
No modern worship songs are named or quoted (copyright).

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'the last psalm' changed to 'Psalm 150' (Orthodox Bibles also have a Psalm 151). Cut the dates 1932, 1940 and 'the late twentieth century', 'thousands of young people', 'every week... by the thousands', 'a stone village church' (Taizé's church is modern), 'churches everywhere' and 'many Orthodox churches'. The listener is no longer told what they will feel ('by the tenth time you stop thinking') or what they did this week.
